But the plan also says the custom version is the "same shape as the library version" (PLAN.md:7-8), and libraries let you hand in your own delay function. So you can keep the curve and drop the five schedulers.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Custom inline means five places that count attempts, compute delays and re-dispatch, each of which can drift and each of which has to hand-roll max-attempts and dead-lettering. Library hooks means the curve lives in one function, and attempts/dead-letter come for free; the risk is the hook not exposing something you need (error type, jitter), which option C checks cheaply.
Recommendation: A because it is the same behavior with one-fifth the surface area, and "full control over the curve" is a custom backoff function, not a custom scheduler. [Layer 1]
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Pros / cons:
A) Library retry hooks + one custom backoff function (recommended) (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
  ✅ Attempt counting, re-dispatch and dead-letter come from code already running in production
  ✅ The delay curve lives in one function you fully own; jitter and caps are one line each
  ❌ If the hook signature lacks something (per-error curves), you adapt to the library's shape
B) Custom inline scheduler as planned (human: ~3-4 days / CC: ~1 hr)
  ✅ No dependency on the library's retry semantics; every behavior is explicit in your code
  ✅ Can do things hooks may not allow, like a different curve per error class
  ❌ Five copies of scheduling logic, plus hand-rolled max-attempts and dead-lettering nobody has planned yet
C) Investigate: bounded read of the library's retry hook API first (human: ~1 hr / CC: ~5 min)
  ✅ Turns "the hook can't do X" from a hunch into a quoted API signature before committing
  ✅ Cheap; leaves R1 pending rather than guessing
  ❌ Delays the decision; every other finding in this review depends on R1's answer
Net: one owned function riding proven infrastructure vs. five owned schedulers for a curve the library already lets you set.

questions.question:
D4 — What bounds does the retry policy get?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md retry framework, finding A1/S4, with R1 = library hooks + shared backoff function already approved.
ELI10: "Exponential backoff" alone is a shape, not a policy. Without a ceiling, attempt 20 waits 12 days. Without jitter, ten thousand jobs that failed together retry together and knock the recovering service back over. Without saying which errors are worth retrying, a receiver that answers "400 bad request" gets the same request five more times. Without a dead-letter step, exhausted jobs vanish quietly. Each fix is one line in the shared function or one library config key.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Under-bounded means retry storms, absurd delays and silent job loss in the first real outage. Over-bounded is not really a risk here; these are constants you tune later.
Recommendation: A because with one shared backoff function each bound costs about a line, and each one prevents a named 3am failure.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=3/10
Pros / cons:
A) Full bounded policy: cap + full jitter + attempt limit + transient-only retry + dead-letter (recommended) (human: ~1 day / CC: ~15 min)
  ✅ Retry storms, unbounded waits, retrying 4xx forever and silent loss are all closed in one function
  ✅ Base, cap and max attempts are named constants, so tuning later is a one-line change
  ❌ Needs an error-classification helper (transient vs terminal) that every worker's errors must map into
B) Exponential with cap and attempt limit; retry every error; library default on exhaustion (human: ~half day / CC: ~5 min)
  ✅ Covers the two worst failures (unbounded delay, infinite retries) with minimal code
  ✅ No error taxonomy to maintain
  ❌ Lockstep retries after a mass failure, and 4xx errors burn every attempt before failing
C) Leave bounds to implementation time (human: 0 / CC: 0 now)
  ✅ Nothing to decide today; the plan stays as written
  ✅ Implementer picks values with the code in front of them
  ❌ Five workers may pick five different answers, and the plan cannot be tested against unstated bounds
Net: a handful of constants and a classifier now vs. discovering the missing ones during an outage.

options.label: A) Full bounded policy (recommended)
options.description: min(cap, base*2^n) with full jitter, max attempts constant, retry transient errors only (5xx/429/timeout/network), dead-letter + alert log on exhaustion.

options.label: B) Cap + attempt limit only
options.description: Exponential with a delay cap and attempt limit; every error retries; library default failed state on exhaustion.

options.label: C) Decide at implementation
options.description: Leave all bounds unspecified in the plan.

questions.question:
D5 — What is the webhook delivery contract once retries exist, and what proves it?
Project/branch/task: `main`, PLAN.md retry framework, finding A2/S2 on `processWebhookJob()` (PLAN.md:16-18).
ELI10: Today a webhook is sent at most once: if it fails, it is gone, but the receiver never sees a duplicate. The moment you retry, that promise is physically impossible to keep: a send can succeed on the receiver's side and then time out on yours, and the retry delivers it twice. So the plan is not "missing a regression test", it is changing the contract without saying so. The standard fix is to send a stable idempotency key with every attempt so receivers can throw away the duplicate, and to write tests that pin the new behavior down.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Receivers double-process events (double charge, double notification) with no way to tell. Or, if you preserve at-most-once by accident, webhooks silently stay unreliable while the other 4 workers gain retries.
Recommendation: A because at-least-once is unavoidable with retries; naming it, keying it and testing it is the complete version. Pick B only if your receivers cannot be asked to dedup.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=3/10
Pros / cons:
A) At-least-once + idempotency key on every attempt + 5 contract tests (recommended) (human: ~2 days / CC: ~30 min)
  ✅ Receivers can dedup deterministically; duplicates become harmless instead of invisible
  ✅ Tests pin: one send on success, same key on retry, 4xx fails fast, timeout-after-send retries, exhaustion dead-letters
  ❌ Contract change must be communicated to webhook consumers (docs / changelog)

# Plan: Multi-tenant Auth Refactor (reviewed)

Reviewed target: `PLAN.md` ("Plan: Multi-tenant Auth Refactor"), repo `gstack-plan-count-JcnhYx`, branch `main`, commit 629f68c.
Review: /plan-eng-review, 2026-09-15. Report file selected per user request.
Note: this repo holds only the plan; no application source was available to probe. Findings cite plan lines; confidence is capped accordingly.

## Context
Auth is being split into two new services (`AuthBroker`, `SessionMint`) sharing a tenant-keyed cache, while the current `legacyAuthFlow()` login path is rewritten. The original plan bundled both into one 12-file change with five new components, no regression coverage for the legacy path, and a module-level mutable cache shared by both services. This review reduced scope to a two-phase strangler cutover and three well-defined components, and pins down the remedies for the shared-state, error-swallowing, regression and IDP-latency issues below.

## Existing contracts retained (unchanged from original)
The existing cache adapter keys entries by tenant ID, issuer, audience, and policy version. It evicts expired tokens and invalidates entries on logout, token revocation, or tenant suspension. `AuthCache` retains these unchanged validity and tenant-key rules; they do not serialize mutations. `AuthCache` is a service-facing facade over that same existing adapter, with one backing cache. The adapter, its invalidation hooks, and their existing tests remain in use unchanged.

## Phasing (accepted: D4)
- **Phase 1 (this PR):** land `AuthBroker`, `SessionMint`, `AuthCache` dark behind a feature flag. `legacyAuthFlow()` keeps serving all traffic untouched.
- **Phase 2 (follow-up PR):** rewrite `legacyAuthFlow()` onto the new services behind the same flag, shipped together with its regression suite. Rollback is one flag flip.

## Architecture (accepted: D5)
Three new components, each with one responsibility:
- `AuthBroker` — validates inbound tokens against the IDP and returns an auth decision.
- `SessionMint` — issues sessions for validated principals.
- `AuthCache` — the single service-facing facade over the existing cache adapter. Absorbs the token persistence role originally assigned to `TokenStore`.
- `RequestPolicy` — a typed value/config object, not a class with behavior.

Both services read and write `AuthCache`. How the instance is shared is decided in R1 below.

```
request ─▶ AuthBroker.validate(token, tenant)
              │  cache hit?  ──▶ AuthCache.get(tenant, issuer, audience, policyVersion)
              │  miss ───────▶ IDP calls (see Performance) ──▶ AuthCache.set(...)
              ▼
         auth decision ─▶ SessionMint.mint(principal, RequestPolicy) ─▶ AuthCache.set(session)
                                                                         ▲
   revoke / logout / suspend ─▶ existing adapter invalidation hooks ─────┘
```

## Code quality
`validateAndDispatch()` is 60 lines with three nested try/catch blocks; each catch swallows a different error class. Remedy pending (R3).

## Tests
Unit and integration coverage for the new components and their success/error paths (original plan). Regression coverage for `legacyAuthFlow()` is required before Phase 2 (IRON RULE); contract pending (R4).

## Performance
Token validation issues 5 sequential API calls to the IDP; parallelization pending (R5), cacheability pending (R6).

Finding: Scope 1, P1, confidence 8/10, PLAN.md:27-28, native reviewer
Plan baseline: rewrite in the same PR, no regression test
Runtime evidence: none available (no source in repo)

# Plan: Settings Page UI redesign

## Context

The Account settings page already ships with a single-column form, four header
actions, a persistent InlineStatus, and two fieldsets. The behavior contract is
accepted and matches the checked-in DESIGN.md. What is left is a set of visual
inconsistencies between the current form and that design system: the primary
action is indistinguishable, spacing drifts between 16/24/32px, the error color
pair fails WCAG AA, form labels use three font sizes, and Save shows no pending
feedback for 2-5 seconds. This plan closes those gaps without any new visual
exploration or component replacement.

Review source: `PLAN.md` on `main` (commit `1f79c88`), reviewed with
`/plan-design-review` against `DESIGN.md`. Text-only review; mockups and outside
voices skipped at the user's request.

## Existing product and accepted behavior
This updates an existing account-settings form using the checked-in DESIGN.md.
The shell and components already exist. Profile and Notifications are the only
sections, with visible headings and associated field labels. The page header
contains the title, a short description, and Save/Reset/Cancel/Export actions.
The existing description is “Manage your display name, email address, and notification preferences.”
Preserve that description verbatim.
Preserve the approved single-column structure and component behavior.
The page title “Account settings” is h1. Profile and Notifications are h2
headings that label their fieldsets via aria-labelledby; no heading level is skipped.
The existing DOM and visual order are:
```text
Persistent app navigation
main: Account settings (h1) + description
  Save | Reset | Cancel | Export
  InlineStatus
  Profile (h2): Display name, Email
  Notifications (h2): Weekly digest, Product tips
```

Journey: a user arrives from account navigation wanting to adjust preferences,
edits the labeled fields, saves, and reads the inline Saved timestamp before
leaving. The feedback preserves confidence that their preferences were stored.
The persistent InlineStatus has role=status, aria-live=polite, aria-atomic=true.
After success it reads “Saved at HH:mm” in the user’s local 24-hour time.
Editing away from a saved value changes its text to “Unsaved changes”, so
dirty state never relies on color or the Save button being enabled. Reverting
all edits or confirming Reset restores the last successful save timestamp.
Before any successful save, unchanged values show blank status text; editing
shows “Unsaved changes”, and reverting or confirming Reset restores blank text.
Failed saves retain “Unsaved changes” alongside the error message.
Initial loading uses the existing form skeleton. A new account sees useful
default preferences as specified in DESIGN.md rather than an empty page. Read failures show Retry.
Save is atomic: all fields persist together or none do, so partial success is
not exposed. Field validation, network failure, and successful-save feedback
use the exact existing DESIGN.md patterns. Preserve unsaved values after errors.
Disable repeat Save submissions while pending. Save and Export are mutually
exclusive: disable both while either is pending. After Save finishes, Export
downloads the latest successfully saved preferences. Reset restores saved values only
after confirmation; Cancel confirms discarding dirty edits before returning to
the previous page; Export downloads the current saved preferences as JSON.
Reset and Cancel are disabled while Save or Export is pending; all four header
actions return to their idle/dirty-state behavior when it settles. While preparing Export, use the existing inline
spinner beside “Exporting…” inside its disabled button, aria-busy=true, with reduced-motion support.
An Export failure uses the existing inline error/retry area and preserves
unsaved fields. Retry repeats Export; success clears only that Export error.
Retry controls are siblings beside the status text, outside its live region.
Visible text stays “Retry”; its aria-label is “Retry save” or “Retry export” for that operation.
The read-failure control follows the same pattern with aria-label “Retry loading”.
The existing router protects dirty edits on every in-app exit, including
persistent app navigation, using the same Cancel confirmation dialog.
Register the browser-native beforeunload warning only while the form is dirty;
remove it when clean. Confirmed in-app navigation uses the existing destination
heading focus behavior; Keep editing returns focus to the attempted exit.
During Save or Export, both request buttons use aria-disabled=true plus an
explicit click/keyboard activation guard, rather than the HTML disabled attribute.
They remain focusable and keep the existing disabled appearance. Reset and
Cancel use HTML disabled during the request. Do not move focus while pending
or after success. On a network error, focus the operation-specific Retry only
if focus is still on the request trigger; never steal focus the user moved.
The existing InlineStatus text stays unchanged while Save is pending:
Unsaved changes for a dirty form, otherwise its saved timestamp or initial
blank text. Pending feedback belongs to the request button; do not repeat
Saving… in the status live region. Success and failure use the outcomes above.
When clean and idle, Reset is disabled because it has nothing to discard,
and Cancel navigates back immediately without a confirmation. When dirty
and idle, Reset and Cancel use their existing discard confirmations. Their
44px geometry is unchanged; the disabled style is separate from pending feedback.
The existing ErrorSummary mounts in the status/error area below the action
group and above Profile. It links each invalid field; focus goes to the first
invalid field and the summary is not a second live region. Preserve that slot.
The existing error/Retry row is inline above 640px with an 8px gap. At 640px
and below, Retry wraps below the text as a full-width 44px ghost button,
outside the live region; long errors fit 320px without horizontal scroll.
The existing Export action names downloads account-settings-YYYY-MM-DD.json
using the local date, with no account identifiers. The browser adds its usual
duplicate-name suffix for repeated exports. Preserve this download behavior.

Responsive behavior: above 640px keep the header action group in one row; at
640px and below, place full-width Save first and the three secondary actions
in one equal-column row below it, preserving DOM/tab order. The form fits 320px
without horizontal scroll, including the secondary actions and their 44px targets.
All controls have visible focus rings and 44px targets. Use semantic fieldsets,
labels, a main landmark and heading order; errors link through aria-describedby.
Focus-visible on every control and dialog action is the existing 2px solid
#1d4ed8 outline, offset 2px on white, with measured contrast above 3:1.
Dialogs trap focus; Escape cancels. Closing while staying on the form restores
focus to the Reset or Cancel trigger. Confirmed navigation uses the existing
destination-main-heading focus behavior. Export remains a
clearly labeled button. Respect reduced motion. No additional visual exploration
or component replacement is part of this established form update.
Retain the existing system-ui, sans-serif font family, including on form controls.

## Planned implementation gaps (review findings and decisions)

Each gap below was an unresolved review finding. DESIGN.md names a matching
token for each, but a token mapping is a proposed fix, not an approved one;
each status moved from PENDING to APPROVED only after its own decision
(D3-D8 in this review session, 2026-09-15).

### Gap 1 — Visual Hierarchy (APPROVED: 1A, Pass 1)
Finding: the "Save" button is rendered with the same size, weight, and color as
three other buttons in the page header (Reset, Cancel, Export). Nothing
tells the user which is the primary action.

Decision (1A): Save is the only filled primary button, `#1d4ed8` background
with white text. Reset, Cancel and Export use the existing neutral ghost Button
variant. This applies at every breakpoint (one row above 640px; full-width Save
above the equal-column secondary row at 640px and below) and in every state:
idle, dirty, pending (aria-disabled, existing disabled appearance), and HTML
disabled. Existing Button variants only; no new component. Verify the filled
button's disabled/pending appearance still reads as the primary and meets
contrast for its label and spinner.

### Gap 2 — Spacing (APPROVED: 4A, Pass 5)
Finding: between sections we have 24px in some places, 32px in others, and
16px in a third: no consistent vertical rhythm.

Decision (4A): apply the DESIGN.md 8px scale everywhere in the form.
- 32px between sections: header block (title, description, action group) to
  the status/error slot; status/error slot to Profile; Profile to Notifications.
- 24px between field groups inside a fieldset (Display name to Email; Weekly
  digest to Product tips), and between an h2 and its first field group.
- 8px label-to-input; 8px between error text and its Retry button above 640px
  (Retry wraps below at 640px and under, keeping 8px above it).
- The status/error slot keeps its 32px rhythm when empty so the form does not
  jump when status text, an error, or the ErrorSummary appears.
All values are multiples of 8; no other vertical gap is introduced.

### Gap 3 — Color (APPROVED: 5A, Pass 5)
Finding: the error message uses red text on a light pink background. Contrast
ratio is approximately 3:1 (below WCAG AA).

Decision (5A): use the DESIGN.md pair `error.text #991b1b` on
`error.surface #fef2f2` for every error presentation: inline field errors,
the network-failure and Export-failure messages in the status/error area, and
the ErrorSummary. Measured contrast is about 7.6:1 (relative luminance 0.076
on 0.910), above WCAG AA 4.5:1 and AAA 7:1 for 16px text. Each error shows the
existing error icon plus explicit text; color is never the only signal. Verify
the Retry ghost button and its 2px `#1d4ed8` focus ring on `error.surface`
meet 4.5:1 (text) and 3:1 (ring) respectively.

### Gap 4 — Typography (APPROVED: 3A, Pass 4)
Finding: we use 14px, 16px, and 18px font sizes across the form labels with no
role behind the choice; 14px sits below the 16px body floor.

Decision (3A): two type roles, per DESIGN.md. 16px for body: the page
description, field labels, helper text, InlineStatus text, error text,
ErrorSummary items, button labels and dialog body. 20px for the Profile and
Notifications h2 section headings. Form controls (text inputs, email input,
switches) inherit 16px and the `system-ui, sans-serif` family rather than a
browser default. No 14px or 18px text remains in the form.

Decision (6A, Pass 7): the h1 “Account settings” is shell-owned and outside
the form's two type roles. Keep its existing rendered size unchanged; do not
apply 20px to it. The implementer verifies the current h1 size before touching
type CSS and leaves it as is. DESIGN.md's “two roles” statement covers the
form only; naming the title role in DESIGN.md is a separate design-system item.

Accepted deviation, not a finding: `system-ui, sans-serif` is the mandated app
font. On this OPERATE surface native expectations beat expression, and the plan
excludes visual exploration; do not replace the font in this update.

### Gap 5 — Motion (APPROVED: 2A, Pass 2)
Finding: the "Save" action takes 2-5 seconds with no loading indicator. Users
see a frozen page.

Decision (2A): while the Save request is pending, the Save button shows the
existing inline spinner beside the label “Saving…”, with aria-busy=true and
aria-disabled=true plus the activation guard already specified. This is the
same pattern Export uses for “Exporting…”. Reduced motion: the spinner uses the
existing non-animated fallback; the “Saving…” text alone carries the state.
The user's edits stay visible; focus does not move; the InlineStatus live
region does not repeat “Saving…”. Not a skeleton: the skeleton remains reserved
for initial load. Reserve a min-width on the Save button so the label change
from “Save” to “Saving…” does not reflow the action row at either breakpoint.
